lab_head_height_svl.notes: Geometry target close to Rawat two-specimen HH/SVL (~.101). Engineering rounding; not a pooled animal estimate.

lab_mass_partition_method.notes: Scale the existing unknown segment fractions separately within tail and non-tail groups. Does not claim validated CoM and intentionally does not fit arbitrary segment densities to CoM gates.

lab_actuator_scaling_method.value: kp, kv, forcerange multiplied by new_mass/legacy_mass
lab_actuator_scaling_method.source: NeuroGecko lab candidate v1 engineering design, 2026-09-05
lab_actuator_scaling_method.notes: Engineering mass scaling, not biological muscle calibration. Joint damping, stiffness, and armature remain legacy estimates; fresh training/tuning still needed.

lab_hip_rot_range_deg.source: CODEX_PROMPT.md +/-15 degree engineering limit based on Iguana proxy
lab_hip_rot_range_deg.notes: Candidate-specific engineering range; not measured E. macularius anatomical ROM.

lab_gait_frequency_hz.source: Legacy checkpoint-compatible controller frequency, retained by user build brief
lab_gait_frequency_hz.notes: Locked engineering frequency, not measured gecko cadence. No frequency optimization permitted in this build.

lab_gait_touchdown_delays.source: McElroy, Hickey & Reilly (2008) ipsilateral limb-phase target + engineered symmetric contralateral offset
lab_gait_touchdown_delays.notes: Touchdown DELAYS from HL, not additive offsets.0.435 is an engineered midpoint of supplied0.43/0.44 targets, not a newly measured mean; half-cycle symmetry is a model choice. Actual contacts still fail the requested phase gate.

com_study_body_mass_kg.notes: Adult female cohort mean39.4g, SEM1.2g. Different body-condition/length cohort from2017; not substituted for our38g population choice.

com_study_svl_m.notes: Source mean121.9mm, SEM2.2mm. Transferring dimensionless CoM targets to106mm is an unverified scaling assumption.

com_study_tail_volume_m3.notes: Original tail mean volume7.8cm^3 measured by liquid displacement. Product of cohortmeanmass and22% divided by this volume is only an approximate bulk-density anchor, not per-segment tissue density.

com_fit_non_tail_mass_bounds.source: NeuroGecko constrained inverse calibration v2 engineering regularizer
com_fit_non_tail_mass_bounds.notes: Broad finite group bounds; bilateral limbs share one total-mass variable. Minimum relative entropy to the v1 mass prior selects one solution among many. No resulting segmentmass is claimed measured.

com_fit_tail_min_mass_fraction.source: NeuroGecko constrained inverse calibration v2 engineering regularizer
com_fit_tail_min_mass_fraction.notes: Positive lower mass guard prevents zero-mass mobile distal segments; not a biological bound.

com_fit_tail_density_guard_factor.source: NeuroGecko constrained inverse calibration v2 engineering guard
com_fit_tail_density_guard_factor.notes: Deliberately generous sensitivity guard, NOT a measured material-density limit. Uses collision capsulevolumes as proxy envelopes; overlap makes summed volume an overestimate. Existing bodyshape/density mismatch remains explicit.

com_fit_density_sensitivity_factors.source: NeuroGecko constrained inverse calibration v2 diagnostic sweep
com_fit_density_sensitivity_factors.notes: Sensitivity cases quantify feasibility and bound choices. A feasible stress case is not evidence that its effective density is biologically correct.

lab_contact_bodyweight_fraction.source: Legacy threshold 0.0564N divided by legacy model weight0.0612kg*9.81m/s^2
lab_contact_bodyweight_fraction.notes: Preserves controller force threshold in bodyweight units. NOT cutaneous mechanoreceptor sensitivity.

lab_height_guard_transition_svl.source: NeuroGecko opt-in lab reward engineering calibration
lab_height_guard_transition_svl.notes: Height guard transition width, not biological tolerance or measured skin clearance.

lab_speed_stride_fraction.source: Engineering midpoint of supplied0.62–0.82SVL stride interval
lab_speed_stride_fraction.notes: Lab reward speed target=0.72*neutralSVL*lockedfrequency. Does not add independent cadence/speed validation.

session2_gate2.source: User Session 2 minimum engineering viability requirements
session2_gate2.notes: Every named limb must pass. Duty .78 is informed by Jagnandan & Higham2017; .435 phase is supplied near-trot target. Tolerances and speed/load cutoffs are engineering gates, not animal confidence intervals. Also require full no-fall rollout and independently measured entrainment.

resting_metabolic_rate_mL_O2_per_g_per_h.units: mL O2 per gram per hour at 30 C
resting_metabolic_rate_mL_O2_per_g_per_h.source: Ha et al. 2017, Experimental Animals 66(2):99-105. Scorecard row: the ONLY direct metabolic measurement of this species. 0.075 +/- 0.011.
resting_metabolic_rate_mL_O2_per_g_per_h.notes: Mass-specific and measured at 30 C, which is inside the preferred body temperature band. Scale to another mass with resting_metabolic_rate_mass_exponent. This one number sets how fast the animal gets hungry, and everything in the energy model rests on it.

resting_metabolic_rate_mass_exponent.source: Allometric exponent the scorecard itself applies to scale 0.075 mL O2/g/h to a 40 g adult, giving 0.064 mL O2/g/h.
resting_metabolic_rate_mass_exponent.notes: Mass-specific metabolic rate falls with body mass. Reproducing the scorecard's own 40 g figure from 0.075 with this exponent is the check that the scaling is being applied the same way.

inter_meal_interval_days.source: Mean inter-meal interval 2.33 days (= 201,600 s), consistent with feeding three times per week.
inter_meal_interval_days.notes: This is the timescale BEHAVIOURAL hunger runs on, and it is a hundredfold shorter than the starvation timescale the tail reserve sets. A 38 g gecko burns about 1.7% of its tail reserve between meals but roughly 71% of a meal's worth of energy, so a drive normalised against the reserve would never make the animal hungry while one normalised against a meal makes it hungry exactly on schedule.

prey_item_wet_mass_kg.source: DERIVED. A feeding is 5% of body weight offered and 54.7% consumed, and the corpus describes one feeding bout as 3 crickets. For a 38 g animal that is 0.038*0.05*0.547 = 1.04 g eaten across three items, so ~0.35 g each.
prey_item_wet_mass_kg.notes: DERIVED from a husbandry offering and a bout size, not from weighing a cricket. It scales with the body mass the offering was expressed as a fraction of, so it is only right for a ~38-40 g animal. Meal energy is linear in it.

endurance_coefficient_hours_at_25C.units: hours (coefficient of t_end = a * v^b, v in KM/H)
endurance_coefficient_hours_at_25C.source: t_end = 0.030 * v^-2.07 hours at 25 C, r^2 = 0.87, v in km/h. Companion fit at 15 C is t_end = 0.013 * v^-1.70, r^2 = 0.83, n=24.
endurance_coefficient_hours_at_25C.notes: NOT E. macularius. Measured in Teratoscincus and a 9 g Coleonyx variegatus. The velocity is in KM/H, not m/s, and reading it as m/s inflates endurance about seventyfold. The units check: the equation gives 62.6 min at 0.050 m/s and the same body of work separately reports locomotion sustained beyond 60 min at that speed.

endurance_exponent_at_25C.source: Exponent of t_end = 0.030 * v^-2.07 hours at 25 C, r^2 = 0.87.
endurance_exponent_at_25C.notes: Steeply negative: endurance collapses with speed. Doubling speed cuts sustainable duration by about a factor of four.

maximum_aerobic_speed_m_s_at_25C.source: VO2max is reached across 0.100-0.158 m/s at 25 C; max aerobic speed is 0.075 m/s at 15 C; locomotion is sustained beyond 60 min at 0.050 m/s.
maximum_aerobic_speed_m_s_at_25C.notes: The LOWER bound of the published VO2max range is used as the ceiling, which is the conservative choice: it starts fatiguing the animal at the earliest speed the literature allows. Below this speed the corpus states locomotion is sustainable indefinitely, so fatigue must not accumulate there. The lab walker moves at 0.055 m/s, well below it, and therefore never fatigues -- which is the correct published behaviour, not an omission.

fatigue_recovery_time_constant_s.source: No recovery-from-fatigue timescale appears anywhere in the corpus, for this species or any proxy.
fatigue_recovery_time_constant_s.notes: INVENTED. The literature says how fast a lizard tires and says nothing at all about how fast it recovers. Ten minutes is an engineering choice of the same order as the endurance times themselves. Any behaviour that depends on recovery rate is resting on this number.

cost_of_transport_mL_O2_per_kg_per_m.units: mL O2 per kg per metre
cost_of_transport_mL_O2_per_kg_per_m.source: Minimum net cost of transport, reported as temperature-INDEPENDENT. Autumn, Weinstein & Full 1994, Physiol. Zool. 67(1):238-262, in an 11.2 g Teratoscincus przewalskii.
cost_of_transport_mL_O2_per_kg_per_m.notes: SPECIES CORRECTED session 9. Confidence downgraded verified -> likely: the schema has no "proxy" level, and using one broke the registry loader, so the nearest honest value is used and the proxy status is stated here instead. This entry said species E_macularius and confidence verified, and both were wrong: 0.73 was measured in Teratoscincus przewalskii, a different FAMILY (Gekkonidae, not Eublepharidae). docs/research/gecko_scorecard.md had it right all along, tagged [TP] and defined there as a proxy "used only for energetics"; the machine-readable registry that the code actually reads did not carry the tag across. No cost of transport, sprint maximum, endurance or thermal performance curve has ever been measured in E. macularius -- NOT_IN_CORPUS. The companion number for Coleonyx variegatus, an actual eublepharid, is Autumn, Farley, Emshwiller & Full 1997, Physiol. Zool. 70(6):660-669, and would be the closer proxy. Temperature independence is itself the published finding: the animal pays the same per metre whether warm or cool, even though how FAST it can go is strongly temperature dependent. At 0.055 m/s a 38 g gecko pays about 110 J/h moving, roughly 2.2x its resting 49.5 J/h.

critical_thermal_maximum_C.notes: The warm side of the thermostat has a published bound. The COLD side does not: CTmin is NOT IN CORPUS at any confidence, for this species or any proxy, so a cold-side threshold would be entirely invented. Recorded here so that asymmetry is visible.

metabolic_q10.source: No metabolic Q10 is published for E. macularius. The corpus contains a Q10 of 2.3 for the reptile ultradian SLEEP-CPG period (Laudakia, Arrhenius) and an engineering suggestion of ~2.5, both explicitly not measurements of this animal's metabolism.
metabolic_q10.notes: null on purpose. The module treats a missing Q10 as 1.0, i.e. no thermal dependence of metabolism, which is certainly wrong but is visibly wrong. Substituting the sleep-period Q10 for a metabolic one would be transplanting a constant between unrelated processes and calling it physiology.

resting_metabolic_rate_reference_mass_g.source: DERIVED. The scorecard states 0.075 mL O2/g/h measured, and 0.064 mL O2/g/h after scaling to a 40 g adult by M^-0.22. Those two numbers pin the mass the 0.075 was measured at: 40 / (0.064/0.075)^(1/-0.22) = 19.5 g.
resting_metabolic_rate_reference_mass_g.notes: The published mass-specific rate is meaningless without the mass it was measured on, and the scorecard does not state it directly. Recovering 19.5 g and then reproducing the scorecard's own 40 g figures (0.064 mL/g/h, 2.56 mL/h, 51.5 J/h against its stated 0.064, 2.54, 51.1) is the check that the allometry is being applied the way the scorecard applied it. Anchoring at 40 g instead -- the obvious mistake -- inflates resting metabolism by 17% and shortens the starvation reserve from 137 days to 117.

oxycalorific_J_per_mL_O2.source: DERIVED from the scorecard's own arithmetic: it states 2.54 mL O2/h = 51.1 J/h for a 40 g adult, so 51.1/2.54 = 20.12 J/mL.
oxycalorific_J_per_mL_O2.notes: Recovering 20.12 from the scorecard's two numbers, against a standard oxycalorific equivalent of about 20.1 J/mL, is an independent check that the published conversion was read correctly.

meal_apparent_dry_matter_digestibility.source: Apparent dry-matter digestibility 71 +/- 4.7 % (crude protein 81 %, fat 65-74 %, calcium 43 %).
meal_apparent_dry_matter_digestibility.notes: Only the dry-matter figure is used. Protein, fat and calcium fractions are recorded here because a nutrient-resolved model would need them and would not be able to invent them.

cricket_energy_kJ_per_g_dry.source: Cricket meal ~17.7 kJ/g dry matter, from a rooster assay, not from a gecko trial.
cricket_energy_kJ_per_g_dry.notes: Energy content of the prey, measured in a bird. Nothing about a gecko changes the calorific content of a cricket, so the proxy is mild, but it is a proxy.

cricket_dry_matter_fraction.source: No dry-matter fraction for crickets appears anywhere in the corpus. 0.30 is an engineering assumption needed to convert a wet meal mass into the dry mass the energy figure is expressed per gram of.
cricket_dry_matter_fraction.notes: INVENTED. Meal energy is linear in this number, so a wrong value scales every meal proportionally. It is isolated as its own entry precisely so that dependence is visible rather than buried inside a meal constant.

meal_offering_fraction_bodyweight.units: fraction of body mass offered per feeding
meal_offering_fraction_bodyweight.source: Husbandry protocol: animals offered 5 % of body weight, fed three times per week.
meal_offering_fraction_bodyweight.notes: A captive husbandry schedule, not a measurement of wild intake.

meal_consumed_fraction_of_offering.notes: What the animal actually ate, not what it was given. The 12.2 % spread is wide and is real between-animal variation.

feeding_events_per_week.source: Husbandry protocol: fed three times per week.
feeding_events_per_week.notes: Used as an independent check on the energy model rather than as an input: one meal should cover roughly the interval to the next one. It does -- about 79 h of resting metabolism against a 56 h interval, a surplus consistent with an animal maintaining condition.

tail_lipid_fraction.units: fraction of tail mass that is lipid
tail_lipid_fraction.source: The scorecard's own tail-reserve estimate assumes 50 % lipid and says so; the lipid fraction itself is not measured anywhere in the corpus.
tail_lipid_fraction.notes: INVENTED, and flagged as such in the scorecard too. The whole energy reserve is linear in it, so the ~140-day starvation figure carries this assumption entirely.

lipid_energy_J_per_g.source: Standard energy density of lipid, used by the scorecard in its tail-reserve derivation.
lipid_energy_J_per_g.notes: A physical constant of fat, not a gecko measurement.

preferred_body_temperature_C.source: Preferred body temperature 29.5-31.9 C (midpoint 30.7) in a 5-45 C gradient. Separately 25.8 C in a thigmothermal gradient with no day/night difference.
preferred_body_temperature_C.notes: TWO published values that disagree by ~5 C because the apparatuses differ: a full thermal gradient gives 29.5-31.9, a thigmothermal (contact-heat) gradient gives 25.8. Body temperature tracks SUBSTRATE temperature at r^2 = 0.97, so this animal is a thigmotherm and the thigmothermal figure may be the more ecologically valid one. The band is used here because the gait and metabolic measurements were taken at ~30 C, inside it.

postprandial_metabolic_peak_multiple.source: Postprandial metabolic rate peaks at 3.7-7.3x pre-feeding, 15-33 h after a meal, returning to baseline at 62-170 h. Another lizard genus, paywalled.
postprandial_metabolic_peak_multiple.notes: Digesting a meal costs a large multiple of resting metabolism, so a naive model that adds meal energy without subtracting the cost of processing it overstates the benefit of eating. NOT implemented yet; recorded so the omission is visible.

activity_onset_after_dark_s.source: 81 min mean (SD 89, range 11-247) from lights-out to first approach of a running wheel. Digirolamo 2024, WikiJournal of Science 7(1):5. One adult female, ~12 y, 14 nights of 940 nm IR video plus 21 days of wheel counts.
activity_onset_after_dark_s.notes: PUBLISHED and THIS SPECIES, and it is n = 1. Treat as a case report, not a population value: the SD of 89 min is larger than the mean and the range spans 11 to 247. It is used because it is the ONLY actograph-style dataset that exists for this animal. No field activity budget for wild E. macularius has ever been published -- no emergence times, no retreat times, no activity/light-level curve.

activity_peak_window_h.source: Behaviour scored during 'the evening peak activity period between 6 p.m. and 11 p.m.', lights off about 18:00. Kronke & Xu 2023, Animals 13(23):3595, n=18 adults.
activity_peak_window_h.notes: PUBLISHED and THIS SPECIES, but CAPTIVE and the window was chosen by the experimenters as much as measured -- they scored when they expected activity. Corroborating in direction only: activity was higher in the first 60 min after lights-out than in the last 75 min before dawn (n=1, Digirolamo 2024), and preferred body temperature rises through the light phase, which Angilletta et al. 1999 propose as what initiates evening emergence.

sleep_cycle_period_s.source: No sleep-cycle period has been established for E. macularius. The species appears in Bergel et al. 2026, Nat Neurosci 29:543-550 -- seven lizard species, sleep-dependent infraslow rhythms conserved across reptiles and mammals -- with n = 2 leopard geckos, both male, 72 g. That paper establishes that this animal sleeps and that its eye movements are measurable (EOG electrodes under each eyelid; it closes them, unlike the tokay). It does not give this project a cycle period it can defend.
sleep_cycle_period_s.notes: null ON PURPOSE. A number exists in the reptile sleep literature for the bearded dragon and it would be easy to borrow, but a cycle period transplanted from an agamid to a eublepharid is exactly the kind of substitution this registry exists to make visible. Recorded as absent so that any module depending on a sleep cycle has to declare it is inventing one.

tongue_flick_baseline_per_min.source: Tongue-flicks in 60 s directed at an odourless control swab, 3.0 +/- 1.0, n=7. Cooper 1995, Herpetological Monographs 9:120-129, compiled in Table 1 of Baeckens, Van Damme & Cooper 2017, J Evol Biol 30(4):627-640.
tongue_flick_baseline_per_min.notes: PUBLISHED and THIS SPECIES. One of very few behavioural numbers that exists for E. macularius at all. The same study found two gekkonids showed neither elevated flicking nor attack to prey chemicals, while this eublepharid did -- the difference is the point.

tongue_flick_prey_per_min.source: Tongue-flicks in 60 s directed at a swab carrying cricket chemicals, 14.57, n=7. Same source as the baseline.
tongue_flick_prey_per_min.notes: PUBLISHED and THIS SPECIES. A 4.9x rise over baseline. THE CRITICAL LIMIT: the assay presents the swab about 1 cm from the snout, IN PLAIN VIEW. It demonstrates that the animal can TELL cricket chemicals from a control. It does NOT demonstrate localisation, and no gecko has ever been shown to find prey by smell alone -- Cooper flagged the missing experiment in 1998 and nobody has done it since. So smell may raise arousal; it must not hand out a direction.

predator_reaction_chemical.source: Antipredator reaction probability to snake scent alone, 0.21. Live-snake test, n=42. Frydlova et al. 2026, Behavioral Ecology 37(4):arag062.
predator_reaction_chemical.notes: PUBLISHED and THIS SPECIES. Factorially: chemical chi2 = 8.098, p < 0.0044; visual chi2 < 0.01, p > 0.9; mechanosensory chi2 < 0.01, p > 0.9. Authors verbatim: the initiation of costly defensive action remains strictly gated by chemoreception.

predator_reaction_visual.source: Antipredator reaction probability to the SIGHT of a live snake alone, 0.07 (95% CI 0.02-0.20). Same study.
predator_reaction_visual.notes: PUBLISHED and THIS SPECIES, and it is the number that indicts a vision-first threat model. Three times lower than scent. Visual and mechanosensory stimuli modulated attention and amplified chemical sampling; neither independently elicited overt defensive behaviour.

shelter_retreat_type.source: Field observation, Salt Range and Potohar Plateau, Pakistan: the animal 'inhabits holes and crevices in gravel-mixed stony terrain', and retreat chambers traced through a demolished stone field wall ran from surface openings through narrow passages into chambers. Verbatim on excavation: 'The lizards apparently had done nothing in the setting of the site' -- the voids are masonry artefacts. Khan, M. S. (2009).
shelter_retreat_type.notes: GREY-FIELD, and flagged loudly. The source is a non-peer-reviewed manuscript by a career field herpetologist, and it is the richest description of wild habitat that exists for this species -- peer-reviewed papers cite it as the natural-history authority. It has no sample sizes, no protocols and no statistics. THIS SPECIES DOES NOT DIG: it uses voids that already exist. So the world gets a rock with a gap under it, not diggable ground. The often-repeated 'tight hide' rule from care sheets has ZERO primary support in this species and no tightness-of-fit experiment has ever been done.

warm_surface_temperature_C.source: Voluntarily maintained body temperature of 30 C for 13.5 h/day when a heat source was available; geckos held at a constant 25 C grew 0.11 g/day against 0.16 for thermoregulating animals. Autumn & De Nardo 1995, J Herpetol 29(2):157-162.
warm_surface_temperature_C.notes: PUBLISHED and THIS SPECIES. Two other studies give 28.2 +/- 0.6 (Angilletta et al. 1999) and 25.8 +/- 1.0 (Werner et al. 2005) using different methods, so the honest model is a DIEL RAMP from about 26 C in the morning to 30 C at dusk rather than a single set point -- Angilletta measured exactly that rise and proposed it as what initiates evening emergence. The warm surface is 30 C because that is the top of the ramp and the value the animal chose when it could choose.

thigmothermy_substrate_correlation.source: Body temperature tracked SUBSTRATE temperature at r2 = 0.97, against terrarium air loggers at 0.92-0.93 and atmospheric at 0.92-0.93. Authors' conclusion verbatim: 'E. macularius relies on absorbing heat from the ground and is thigmothermic.' Hastings et al. 2023, Biology Open 12(10):bio060114. n = 12 adults, IR thermography plus iButton loggers, 25 -> 15 -> 25 C over 7 h.
thigmothermy_substrate_correlation.notes: PUBLISHED, THIS SPECIES, and it refutes how this project modelled basking. The animal does not take heat from light -- it takes it from the GROUND, by lying on it. Melanistic pigment had no effect on heating rate (r2 = -0.08, P = 0.68), which is further evidence against radiation-driven warming. So the world needs a warm SURFACE, not a lamp, and the 'bask' behaviour channel is named for a mechanism this animal does not use.

shelter_choice_beats_safety.source: Given a choice between safe COOL shelter and an exposed HEATED open area, geckos 'selected heat sources over shelters'. Substrate moisture also emerged as a significant factor in shelter choice, and temperature may act as an activity cue alongside the light cycle. Craioveanu, Craioveanu & Miresan 2017, Zoo Biology 36(4):273-277, n = 8 juveniles.
shelter_choice_beats_safety.notes: PUBLISHED and THIS SPECIES, but n = 8 JUVENILES and the paper is paywalled -- the actual temperatures, humidities and time budgets could not be read, only the abstract's conclusion. It matters because it is a measured conflict between two drives, which is exactly what an action-selection model should have to resolve. Corroborating in another genus: 9 Gehyra species, n = 85, used a humid crevice for under 10 % of crevice time whenever the dry alternative was warmer.

prey_velocity_peak_deg_s.source: Four independent lineages land in the same band. Bufo bufo prey-catching turning peaks 30-60 deg/s and falls to zero above ~200 (Ewert 1969). Crotalus atrox IR tectal units: almost no response at 5 deg/s, maximum ~50, declining by 120 (Kaldenbach, Bleckmann & Kohl 2016). Mouse looming escape is released only at 35 deg/s (Yilmaz & Meister 2013). Zebrafish hunting uses 30-60 deg/s.
prey_velocity_peak_deg_s.notes: PUBLISHED in four separate clades, and the pit viper is the closest -- a squamate, same tectum. This is the single most robust cross-species number found in the whole vision search. It is NOT measured in any gecko: no lizard tectum has ever had its velocity tuning recorded. The midpoint of the toad band is used because the pit viper peak sits inside it.

prey_velocity_low_cut_deg_s.source: IR-sensitive tectal units respond almost not at all at 5 deg/s. Kaldenbach, Bleckmann & Kohl 2016, J Comp Physiol A 202(6):389-398.
prey_velocity_low_cut_deg_s.notes: PUBLISHED, squamate, and the authors draw the behavioural conclusion themselves: a motionless snake cannot detect a stationary or slowly moving object, and must reveal it with scanning head movements. That is the honest justification for a low cut, and also the reason a tectum alone is correctly blind to frozen prey.

prey_velocity_high_cut_deg_s.source: Prey-catching turning response falls to zero above ~200 deg/s. Ewert 1969, Pflugers Archiv 308:225-243.
prey_velocity_high_cut_deg_s.notes: PUBLISHED but recovered through secondary sources -- Springer blocked direct retrieval of the 1969 paper, so the figure is transcribed rather than read. An amphibian, and the upper cut is the least transferable end of the curve: gecko critical flicker fusion is reported around 20 Hz, which would put a much lower ceiling on what this animal can resolve, but that figure could not be traced to a primary source either. Treat as an engineering ceiling, not a gecko measurement.

prey_elevation_switch.source: Identical stimulus, opposite behaviour by elevation. Overhead loom: escape 42/56 = 75%, latency 0.45 s. Same loom to the side: 53%, latency 1.79 s. Overhead sweep: freeze 56%. Same sweep to the side: escape 5%, and the mouse APPROACHED the screen on 80% of trials. Solomon, Janbon, Bimson & Wheatcroft 2023, R Soc Open Sci 10(4):230034. Yilmaz & Meister 2013 found floor-mounted looms produced ZERO escapes.
prey_elevation_switch.notes: PUBLISHED, mammal, and anatomically grounded: medial superior colliculus carries the upper visual field and projects to the escape and freeze pathways, lateral SC carries the lower field and projects to zona incerta for hunting. The ecological logic -- raptors above, insects below -- applies at least as strongly to a small nocturnal terrestrial insectivore, but NO reptile has been tested. The switch sits at the horizon because that is where the anatomy divides, not because a boundary was measured.

strike_trigger_distance_m.source: Starting distance to prey at strike onset, 2.03 +/- 0.08 cm, n=5 juveniles, 500 fps, crickets. Vollin & Higham 2021, Integr Comp Biol 61(2):538-549, doi:10.1093/icb/icab076.
strike_trigger_distance_m.notes: PUBLISHED but NOT this species. Eublepharidae, same family, but juveniles of a much smaller gecko. Adults of the same species strike from a mean 14.6 mm on non-scorpion prey (Whitford et al. 2022, n=9), so the juvenile figure is the LONGER of the two and is the conservative choice for a trigger. No strike distance has ever been measured in E. macularius: the only feeding kinematics for the target species is Delheusy, Brillet & Bels 1995 at 64 fps, which could not resolve the capture phase and excluded it from every table.

strike_peak_speed_m_s.source: Maximum strike velocity 85.1 +/- 2.19 cm/s, pre-autotomy, n=5 juveniles. Vollin & Higham 2021.
strike_peak_speed_m_s.notes: PUBLISHED, wrong species. Note the scale of what this buys: the walker moves at 0.055 m/s and the cricket escapes at 0.093-0.143 m/s, so the strike is roughly 15x the walk and 6-9x the prey's escape. That ratio is why a real gecko catches an animal it cannot outrun, and why a pursuit-only hunter in this codebase could never succeed.

strike_peak_acceleration_m_s2.source: Maximum acceleration 46.6 +/- 1.97 m/s^2, pre-autotomy. Vollin & Higham 2021.
strike_peak_acceleration_m_s2.notes: PUBLISHED, wrong species. Peak acceleration occurs 16.34 +/- 6.71 ms BEFORE contact and peak velocity 9.03 +/- 5.75 ms before contact, so the animal is already decelerating when it arrives.

strike_distance_speed_correlation_r.source: Attack distance vs maximum strike velocity, r = 0.47, P = 0.009, n=9 adults, 29 trials. Whitford, Freymiller, Higham & Clark 2022, Biol J Linn Soc 135(3):533-540, doi:10.1093/biolinnean/blab167.
strike_distance_speed_correlation_r.notes: PUBLISHED, wrong species, and the single most useful relationship found in the whole hunting literature: a longer strike is a FASTER strike. It gives a controller a real scaling law instead of a constant. r=0.47 is a moderate correlation -- it explains about 22% of the variance, so the scaling is a tendency and not a rule, and the residual spread is real animal variability that a deterministic model discards.

strike_capture_success.source: Capture success on evasive crickets, 116/140 trials = 82.9 %, n=5. Vollin & Higham 2023, Front Behav Neurosci 17:1173065, doi:10.3389/fnbeh.2023.1173065. Non-evasive mealworms: 53/53 = 100 %.
strike_capture_success.notes: PUBLISHED, wrong species. A model that never misses has been fitted to the harness rather than the animal: the real animal misses roughly one strike in five on evasive prey. Unaffected by tail autotomy (77.0 % intact vs 78.6 % post-autotomy in the 2021 study), which is why the miss rate is modelled as a property of the strike rather than of the body.

strike_duration_s.source: Representative capture cycle, Fig. 2: total open-close cycle about 80 ms with peak gape about 37 degrees at 47 ms. Delheusy, Brillet & Bels 1995, Amphibia-Reptilia 16(2):185-201, doi:10.1163/156853895X00361. n=6 adult males, SVL 120 +/- 4 mm, 64 fps, 22 mm Gryllus bimaculatus.
strike_duration_s.notes: THE ONLY STRIKE-PHASE NUMBER THAT COMES FROM THE TARGET SPECIES, and it is read off a figure rather than a table. That paper could only digitise 5 lateral capture cycles from 2 animals -- insufficient for quantitative analysis -- so capture is described qualitatively there and excluded from Table 1. At 64 fps one frame is 15.6 ms, so an 80 ms cycle spans about 5 frames. Treat as an order of magnitude. Confidence uncertain deliberately.

prey_flee_speed_reference_m_s.source: The walker's own steady speed, used as the reference at which the published flee radius applies.
prey_flee_speed_reference_m_s.notes: INVENTED, AND IT EXISTS BECAUSE THE MODEL WAS UNWINNABLE WITHOUT IT. The prey fled at a FIXED 0.075 m radius regardless of how the predator approached, while the strike must be launched from 0.0203 m and the prey escapes at 0.118 m/s against a 0.055 m/s walk. Measured over 60 s of pursuit: closest approach 51.1 mm, zero strikes. The gecko could not physically reach striking distance by any route, so adding a strike was necessary and not sufficient. The real animal closes that gap by STALKING -- the published E. macularius ethogram names `walk slow motion` as 'walking with a strongly reduced speed, mostly in context of prey capture' (Kronke & Xu 2023, n=18) -- and a prey that cannot tell a creep from a charge makes that behaviour meaningless. The DIRECTION is well supported: flight initiation distance rises with approach speed across the antipredator literature, and crickets specifically detect approaching predators through cercal air-current receptors, where a faster approach produces a larger signal. The MAGNITUDE here is invented. Any capture rate this model produces depends on it.

prey_flee_speed_exponent.source: Engineering choice. Linear scaling of flee radius with approach speed.
prey_flee_speed_exponent.notes: INVENTED. No published function relates cricket flight-initiation distance to predator approach speed. Linear is the least-assuming monotone choice; the true relationship is unmeasured and could be threshold-like, since cercal interneurons have firing thresholds rather than proportional outputs. Recorded as the specific thing to replace if anyone measures it.

prey_flee_radius_floor_m.source: Engineering floor, set below the 0.0203 m strike trigger distance.
prey_flee_radius_floor_m.notes: INVENTED. Without a floor an arbitrarily slow approach would let the gecko walk its mouth onto the prey unnoticed, which would make capture success 100 % and would be fitting the harness rather than the animal -- the published rate on evasive crickets is 82.9 %. The floor sits just inside strike range so that a perfect stalk still only BUYS A STRIKE rather than a meal, and the strike can still miss.

prey_ambient_speed_m_s.source: Half the low end of the escape-speed band (0.093 m/s). No published walking speed for an undisturbed cricket exists anywhere in the corpus, for Acheta or Gryllus, on any substrate.
prey_ambient_speed_m_s.notes: INVENTED, and it exists because its ABSENCE was worse. FleeingPrey.step only moved the prey inside the 0.075 m flee radius, while detection range is 0.30-0.50 m, so prey_total_travel_mm measured 0.0 across 1800 frames -- the tectum is a motion detector and it was pointed at a stationary object (ledger #135). A cricket that never moves is not a conservative choice, it is a wrong one. Half the escape speed is an ordering claim (an undisturbed animal moves slower than a fleeing one) rather than a measurement, and any result that depends on the exact value must say so.

prey_ambient_move_fraction.source: Engineering choice. No move/pause bout structure is published for any cricket.
prey_ambient_move_fraction.notes: INVENTED. Crickets walk in bouts rather than continuously, and a prey that glides at constant velocity would be both unrealistic and unrealistically EASY for a motion detector -- constant motion is the easiest possible signal. The one structural insight the corpus does carry is from Teratoscincus, not a cricket: pause length should be sampled conditional on the preceding move length. That refinement is not implemented and its absence is recorded here.

prey_ambient_turn_rate_rad_s.notes: INVENTED. How sharply an undisturbed cricket changes heading is unmeasured. Set so a walking bout curves visibly within a second rather than tracking a straight line, because a straight-line walker is again the easy case for a motion detector.

prey_escape_speed_m_s.source: DERIVED, not published: escape dash length 28-43 mm and dash duration ~0.3 s appear separately in docs/research/strategy_v1.md; the corpus never prints their quotient. Midpoint 35.5 mm / 0.3 s = 0.118 m/s.
prey_escape_speed_m_s.notes: NO published cricket escape SPEED exists anywhere in the corpus. This is a quotient of two separately reported quantities and must never be cited as a measured escape speed. Range implied by the endpoints is 0.093-0.143 m/s. Note the consequence: the lab walker moves at 0.055 m/s, so prey fleeing at this speed CANNOT be run down. That is biologically correct -- capture success 82.9% on evasive prey is achieved by a strike at 0.851 m/s from 2.03 cm, not by pursuit -- and it means a hunting gate is meaningless until a strike behaviour exists.

prey_flee_radius_m.source: Engineering trigger distance; the corpus's own suggestion is 'gecko head within ~5-10 cm and closing', itself tagged as a finite-state-machine design choice rather than a measurement.
prey_flee_radius_m.notes: No published distance at which a cricket initiates escape from an approaching gecko. Midpoint of the corpus's own 5-10 cm engineering suggestion. It is deliberately larger than the 2.03 cm strike trigger distance so that prey reacts before the gecko is in strike range, which is what makes the prey evasive at all.

prey_escape_latency_s.source: Published escape-response latency: 70-86 ms tethered, ~104 ms free-walking.
prey_escape_latency_s.notes: Midpoint of the tethered band. The free-walking figure is longer (~104 ms) and is arguably the better match for an unrestrained cricket; 85 ms is the more conservative choice because a shorter latency makes the prey harder, not easier. Modelled as a fixed delay, not the corpus's suggested N(85,40) ms distribution, because a distribution would need a threat-speed dependence that has no measured form.

prey_capture_distance_m.source: Strike trigger distance for evasive prey, 2.03 +/- 0.08 cm = 0.384 SVL, scaled to this body's 0.106 m SVL.
prey_capture_distance_m.notes: This is the distance a real gecko LAUNCHES A STRIKE from, not the distance at which prey is in its mouth. It is used as the capture proxy only because no strike behaviour exists yet; the moment one does, this becomes the strike trigger and capture becomes the outcome of the strike. Recording it this way keeps the substitution visible instead of burying a generous capture radius. For contrast, the brain environment's existing eat_radius is 0.10 m, roughly five times this distance.

prey_radius_m.source: Sphere proxy. Published prey size is 15-20 mm for a ~50 mm SVL gecko = 0.30-0.40 SVL; at 0.35 SVL this body's prey is ~37 mm long. The sphere radius is a crude stand-in for that body, not a measured dimension.
prey_radius_m.notes: A sphere is not a cricket. Radius chosen so the prey subtends a visual angle in the same range as the published prey rather than to match any measured dimension. Prey shape, legs, antennae and the way a cricket's silhouette changes as it turns are all absent.

prey_arena_radius_m.source: Engineering bound on where prey may be placed and how far it may flee.
prey_arena_radius_m.notes: Not an enclosure size. Published arenas are far larger -- McElroy 2008 used a 5.2 m racetrack -- and terrarium size has a published null effect on activity (P = 0.926). This radius exists so prey stays inside the camera's world during a 20-300 s episode, and should be revisited when a real enclosure with shelter is built.

prey_visible_prey_note.source: Capture success 82.9% overall on evasive crickets (77.0% intact, 78.6% post-autotomy, not significantly different); 100% (53/53) on non-evasive mealworms.
prey_visible_prey_note.notes: Do not push a hunting policy to 100% on evasive prey: the real animal misses roughly one in five. A model that never misses has been fitted to the harness rather than the animal.

lab_base_parameters.units: normalized actuator half-ranges except tuck radians and heading_gain per radian
lab_base_parameters.source: Session 2 manual trial19_front_height; experimental candidate, Gate2 FAIL
lab_base_parameters.notes: Engineering choices, not neural/muscle data. Selected for >.04m/s, >.8 net/path and low swing loads, not as a biological optimum. Fore/hind.54 is an angular-command proxy inspired by published44.41/82.57, not anatomical validation. Continuous front mode disables seek/relax. Heading input changes left/right amplitudes with clipped gain. Live default remains legacy. Previous lab control can be reconstructed with versioned test/evidence parameters and profile. Session 3g: spine_amp/tail_amp/tail_phase_lag moved into this set at their existing constructor defaults (0.30/0.15/0.15), so behaviour is unchanged; they are now overridable per run for fitting. Session 4: hind_sprawl_amplitude/fore_sprawl_amplitude/sprawl_phase drive femur and humerus depression, which were commanded flat (measured excursion 0.95 and 1.16 deg against published 52.42+/-3.25 and 101.38+/-15.88); tail_hindlimb_coupling makes hind fore-aft amplitude depend on realised tail motion, standing in for the caudofemoralis, whose origin on the caudal vertebrae is why blocking the tail collapses hindlimb excursions in Jagnandan & Higham 2017. The sprawl amplitudes and phase default to 0.0, exactly the pre-Session-4 behaviour. tail_hindlimb_coupling defaults to 0.36, fitted so that removing tail drive reproduces Jagnandan & Higham 2017: femur retraction -20.7% against a published -21%, ankle -16.5% against -17%, forelimb and hind duty factor unchanged. Knee moves +3.8% where the paper reports -11%, and that miss is recorded rather than tuned away. At the reference tail_amp the coupling gain is exactly 1.0, so the intact gait is bit-identical to the pre-Session-4 base and only the ablation response changes; the waveform shapes are INVENTED and only the peak-to-peak excursions they are tuned against are published.

lab_total_power_effort_alpha.notes: Engineering starting coefficient only. No training performed; no causal correlation claim. Legacy remains zero.

diagnostic_phase_bins.notes: Display resolution, not an event detector or biological property.

contact_period_cv_ceiling.notes: Strictly less than this value; never used to edit raw contacts or merge measured cycles.

entrainment_tolerance_fraction.notes: Observed same-foot complete-cycle rate must lie within 10 percent of commanded cadence. Does not merge or select cycles to make a controller pass.

contact_cycle_warning_ratio.notes: Warn when complete same-foot contact-cycle rate lies outside [1/2,2] times the recorded commanded frequency. Not a biological acceptance gate. Never removes, merges or relabels measured cycles to fit the oscillator.

emg_hindlimb_preautotomy.source: Jagnandan & Higham (2018), J Exp Biol221:jeb179564, Table3, https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.179564
emg_hindlimb_preautotomy.notes: Root visually verified supplied PDFTable3; n10cohort, per-muscle subset not assumed. SEMs in source-table percent: CF onset2.26,duration2.00,peak3.08,amp9.04; G1 onset2.30,duration4.26,peak5.49,amp5.12; G2 onset2.31,duration1.56,peak1.28,amp5.90. Smoothstep envelope SHAPE is an invented interpolation, not observed waveform or force. Table1 is stanceRIA, not timing. PDFSHA256008ee101c9a00a1a873ad83e558244489c84ef7a045622d5d5be0142921de1cc.
